method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)' (published 29 September 2025), 17 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12477467). S2: QUOTED from Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9) 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)' (published 2021 (2020 update)), 6 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC8116237). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. The source is a guideline-adherence score that summarises the ECIL (haematology), AST-IDCOP (solid organ transplant) and US IDSA/NIH (HIV) PJP guidelines; those guidelines themselves were paywalled (ECIL) or bot-blocked (NIH OI guidelines at clinicalinfo.hiv.gov, HTTP 403) and were not read. WikEM's PJP page (CC BY-SA) was read but held its drug regimens in an unexpanded template, so this open ECMM summary was used instead. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the AGIHO/DGHO 2020 prophylaxis guideline (CC BY 4.0, quoted), for primary prophylaxis in haematology and oncology; the S1 claims are unchanged. Australian candidates were tried first and could not be read: the 2014 Australasian PJP consensus (Intern Med J, doi 10.1111/imj.12599; Wiley returned HTTP 403), eviQ (the page served an empty script shell), and again the ECIL 2016 prevention guideline (OUP bot challenge) and the NIH OI guideline (HTTP 403).

claims.claim: **HIV:** risk rises in people who are not on (or not adherent to) antiretroviral therapy and have a CD4 count under 200 cells/mm³.
claims.source_text: Patients with HIV are at increased risk if ART-naive and ART non-adherent and showing a CD4 cell count <200 cells/mm3.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Without HIV, the highest risk is after haematopoietic stem cell transplant (especially beyond day 100) and lung or kidney transplant.** Moderate risk: cancer or autoimmune disease on combined immunosuppression including glucocorticoids (median 30 mg prednisone-equivalent daily for 2–3 months or more). B-cell-depleting drugs appear to carry moderate to high risk; a single immunomodulator carries low risk.
claims.source_text: Current data show that patients at high risk of PCP are haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients (particularly >100 days post-transplant) and lung or kidney transplant recipients., Patients at moderate risk are patients with malignancies or autoimmune diseases receiving a combination of immunosuppressive therapy including glucocorticoids with a median dose of 30 mg prednisone equivalent daily for at least 2-3 months. Patients treated with a single immunomodulating drug are at low risk., An exception are patients treated with B cell-depleting agents, who seem to be at moderate to high risk.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Classic triad: breathlessness, fever and dry cough, often with tachypnoea and hypoxia.** People with HIV usually have the triad; people without HIV present less specifically, more often with breathlessness and respiratory failure, and deteriorate faster.
claims.source_text: Besides the symptom triad of dyspnoea, fever and dry cough, additional tachypnoea and hypoxia contribute to the suspicion of PCP. Patients infected with HIV present the symptom triad regularly, whereas non-HIV-infected patients show less specific symptoms, with dyspnoea and respiratory failure being more common. … In patients without HIV infection, there is rapid respiratory failure with many inflammatory cells detected in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and fewer asci present.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Imaging:** bilateral symmetric reticular shadowing on chest X-ray; on CT, ground-glass opacity with peripheral sparing, thickened interlobular septa and crazy paving.
claims.source_text: Radiographic imaging shows characteristic features, with bilateral symmetric reticular opacities in chest X-rays, and ground glass opacities with peripheral sparing, thickened interlobular septae, and the crazy paving phenomenon with CT.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **PJP is more lethal without HIV:** attributable mortality is 21.9–22.8% in non-HIV patients versus 3.1–9.9% in people with HIV.
claims.source_text: The PCP-attributed mortality among non-HIV patients is estimated at 21.9%-22.8% compared with 3.1%-9.9% among patients living with HIV.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bronchoalveolar lavage is the best sample for everyone.** Induced sputum performs comparably in HIV but less consistently without HIV; nasopharyngeal swabs and expectorated sputum have low sensitivity and are a last resort.
claims.source_text: BALF is the sample with the highest sensitivity and specificity [e.g. conventional PCR (cPCR) sensitivity 97.2%, specificity 95.4%] for both HIV and non-HIV populations. Induced sputum (IS) has comparable test performance for individuals infected with HIV (e.g. cPCR sensitivity 95.6%, specificity 91.7%). In contrast, for non-HIV patients the results are less consistent. Two meta-analyses (Brown et al. and Senécal et al.) evaluated PCR diagnostics in BALF and IS. Brown et al. did not report relevant differences for cPCR and quantitative PCR (qPCR) performed on these samples, whereas Senécal et al. found reduced specificity, particularly in IS. We therefore assigned three points for using BALF and two points for IS. Nasopharyngeal swabs or expectorated sputum have low sensitivity and therefore should only be used when no other options are feasible.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Immunofluorescence microscopy is the standard test;** conventional stains are less sensitive. A negative microscopy result does not exclude PJP, especially without HIV.
claims.source_text: The standard microbiological test to detect the pathogen can be achieved via visualization of asci and trophic forms of P. jirovecii by immunofluorescence (IF). We valued the procedures with three points. Direct staining of BALF with May-Grünwald, Wright-Giemsa or Grocott-Gömöri methenamine silver stain is less sensitive and these techniques are therefore awarded two points. It is important to note that negative microscopy does not rule out PCP, especially in patients without HIV, because they appear to have fewer asci and trophic forms present in the lung.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PCR is highly sensitive (negative predictive value 100%) but cannot reliably separate infection from colonisation;** no validated cycle-threshold cut-off exists.
claims.source_text: Recently, more data have become available on the use of PCR techniques demonstrating a high sensitivity and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 100%. As a result we allocated three points for this. Higher fungal loads are associated with low cycle threshold (ct) values, but until now no validated cut-off values have been determined to differentiate infection from colonization.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Raised LDH and serum beta-D-glucan support the diagnosis;** interpret beta-D-glucan against co-medications and co-infections, and it is unclear whether a negative result excludes PJP without HIV.
claims.source_text: Another indicator suggestive of PCP is an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). We therefore allocated one point for the laboratory testing of LDH. Alongside LDH, elevated β-D-glucan (BDG) in serum also supports suspicion for PCP infections. Hence, BDG measurement was weighted with two points. However, it is important to emphasize that although both markers may aid in the diagnostic process, interpretation of BDG results has to occur in the context of the patient's comedications and potential coinfections. Furthermore, in non-HIV patients, data remain sparse and it is still unclear whether a negative BDG reliably rules out PCP.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First line is co-trimoxazole: trimethoprim 15–20 mg/kg plus sulfamethoxazole 75–100 mg/kg.** Oral is fine for mild and moderate disease when absorption is not impaired; give it IV in moderate to severe disease and switch to oral once improving. Treat for at least 14 days if moderate and 21 days if severe.
claims.source_text: The first-line treatment for PCP is trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, also known as co-trim, septrin or bactrim, administered at a dosage of trimethoprim 15-20 mg/kg and sulfamethoxazole 75-100 mg/kg. An oral administration route is appropriate in mild and moderate cases without factors impairing gastrointestinal absorption. In moderate to severe cases, IV application is recommended and an oral administration can be considered once the patient's clinical condition is improving. Treatment duration should be at least 14 days in moderate cases and 21 days in severe cases.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Alternatives (weaker evidence):** pentamidine 4 mg/kg/day; primaquine 30 mg/day with clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly; atovaquone 750 mg every 8–12 hours; or dapsone 100 mg with a second drug at 15 mg/kg/day. Before switching, judge whether co-trimoxazole side effects can be managed.
claims.source_text: For alternative treatments, such as pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day), primaquine/clindamycin (30 mg/day + 600 mg every 8 h), atovaquone (750 mg every 8-12 h daily) and dapsone (100 mg plus 15 mg/kg/day), we allocated two points. Prior to switching to second-line treatments, a thorough evaluation should determine whether the adverse events of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole are manageable, as evidence supporting alternative regimes is limited.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Co-trimoxazole side effects are common (20–80%):** rash (rarely Stevens–Johnson syndrome), fever, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, azotaemia and hyperkalaemia. Treat mild reactions symptomatically; stop and switch for severe or life-threatening ones.
claims.source_text: Adverse effects of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole are frequent (20%-80%) and include rashes (rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome), fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, azotaemia and hyperkalaemia. Mild reactions can be managed symptomatically with antihistamines, antiemetics and antipyretics. In case of severe reactions or life-threatening events, therapy should be discontinued and switched to alternative therapies.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Adjunctive corticosteroids for moderate to severe PJP in HIV,** started as early as possible and tapered per guideline; they reduce mortality. Without HIV they are not routine but may be considered case by case in respiratory failure.
claims.source_text: In this population, the use of adjunctive corticosteroids has been shown to improve the overall mortality in cases with moderate to severe PCP. Prednisone should be initiated as soon as possible and tapered according to current guideline recommendations. … In contrast, adjunctive corticosteroids are not routinely recommended in PCP patients without HIV infection. However, in case of respiratory failure they might be considered on an individual basis.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In HIV, start antiretroviral therapy within 2 weeks of the PJP diagnosis;** early start was non-inferior or superior to delay.
claims.source_text: newer studies revealed that early initiation of ART was non-inferior or superior to delayed initiation with regards to outcome. Therefore, ART should ideally be started within 2 weeks of diagnosing PCP.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Prophylaxis is strongly recommended for three groups:** acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, fludarabine–cyclophosphamide–rituximab, and allogeneic stem cell transplant, plus anyone on long-term steroids above 20 mg a day prednisone-equivalent for 4 weeks. It prevents PJP (A-I) and lowers mortality (A-IIr).
claims.source_text: Oncologic patients at significant risk for PcP are those treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, those treated with a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab [], and patients undergoing allogeneic HSCT [, ]. Moreover, long-term use of steroids (> 20 mg/day prednisone equivalent for 4 weeks) increases the risk of developing PcP [, ]. Patients with hematologic malignancies appear to have higher mortality rates once they develop PcP []. The administration of chemoprophylaxis in patients with one of these three risk factors is thus strongly recommended to prevent PcP (A-I) and reduce mortality (A-IIr).
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Moderate-risk patients may or may not be given prophylaxis (C-III):** for example R-CHOP14 or escalated BEACOPP, nucleoside analogues, long-term anti-CD20 antibodies, high-dose steroids with brain radiotherapy, or a CD4 count under 200 cells/μl. No study shows benefit in these groups.
claims.source_text: Other hematologic and oncologic patients may occasionally develop PcP, such as lymphoma patients treated with R-CHOP14 or escalated BEACOPP protocol, patients treated with nucleoside analogs or long-term anti-CD20 antibody therapy, patients receiving high-dose steroids in addition to a radiotherapy for brain malignancies, and patients with CD4 count < 200 cells/μl [, ]. There are no studies demonstrating benefit of PcP chemoprophylaxis in these patient groups, though it is likely that the number needed to treat is considerably higher compared to the high-risk groups. Such patients at moderate risk may or may not receive chemoprophylaxis to prevent PcP (C-III) and to reduce mortality (C-III).
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Some drugs mandate prophylaxis:** give it with idelalisib (from the start, continuing 2–6 months after stopping), with temozolomide plus radiotherapy, and with alemtuzumab (A-IIu,t).
claims.source_text: Patients receiving idelalisib are at high risk for developing PcP and prophylaxis must be administered concurrently (drug label) [-]. Initiation of chemoprophylaxis at the beginning of therapy is recommended by the manufacturer and should be maintained for 2-6 months after stopping therapy. … Based on the documented high-risk situation, we strongly recommend chemoprophylaxis against PcP for patients receiving temozolomide (in combination with radiotherapy), idelalisib, or alemtuzumab (A-IIu,t)
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Co-trimoxazole is the first-choice prophylaxis (A-IIt,r)** and also covers toxoplasmosis and nocardiosis. Any of these schedules is acceptable (B-IIt): one single-strength tablet (80/400 mg) daily, or one double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) daily or three times a week; in HIV, thrice-weekly double strength cut stopping for side effects by 43%.
claims.source_text: Based on the available evidence, the most effective prophylactic agent is TMP-SMX, which also offers protection for toxoplasmosis [], nocardiosis [], and actinomycosis. For these reasons, TMP-SMX is the first-choice agent for PcP prophylaxis (A-IIt,r). It is unknown whether the low doses of TMP-SMX used for PcP prophylaxis are also effective in preventing other infections. No relevant differences in efficacy of different dosing strategies for TMP-SMX, i.e., one single-strength tablet per day (80/400 mg) or one double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) daily or thrice a week, were shown in clinical studies [, ]. A study in HIV-infected patients observed a 43% lower risk of discontinuing TMP-SMX due to side effects if the double-strength tablet was given thrice a week instead of daily []. We recommend using any of these dosing regimens (B-IIt).
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If co-trimoxazole is not tolerated, atovaquone 1500 mg once daily with a fatty meal is the first alternative** (A-IIt; lower doses work less well). Dapsone 100 mg a day is an option when blood toxicity is not a concern (A-IIt): test for G6PD deficiency first and watch for methaemoglobinaemia.
claims.source_text: In patients with intolerance or severe adverse events related to TMP-SMX administration, atovaquone, dapsone, or pentamidine (aerosolized) can be used as alternatives. Atovaquone has been studied in HIV-infected patients [-], while only few studies in non-HIV-infected immunocompromised patients exist [-]. The drug was highly effective, generally well tolerated and not associated with hematologic toxicity. We therefore recommend atovaquone as first alternative to TMP-SMX as PcP prophylaxis in patients with underlying hematologic or oncologic malignancies. Low-dose atovaquone has been described to be less effective in PcP prophylaxis []; thus, 1500 mg atovaquone should be administered once daily (off-label use) (A-IIt). To increase bioavailability of atovaquone, it should be taken during a fatty meal [, ]. If hematologic toxicity is not a major concern, dapsone (100 mg/day) can be used (A-IIt). Efficacy of daily dapsone was equivalent to the administration of TMP-SMX in comparative studies [-]. Testing for glucose-6-phosphat dehydrogenase deficiency is recommended prior to administration of dapsone. If prophylaxis of toxoplasmosis is indicated, dapsone should be combined with pyrimethamine. The risk of dapsone-induced methemoglobinemia must be carefully considered.
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Aerosolised pentamidine 300 mg once a month** is a moderate recommendation (B-IIt): no blood toxicity or interactions, but probably less effective, no cover for toxoplasmosis or bacteria, and staff exposure needs protecting against.
claims.source_text: Aerosolized pentamidine is a popular option for PcP prophylaxis, considering the lack of hematologic toxicity or drug-drug interactions and the long dosing interval of 28 days. However, efficacy is probably lower compared to systemic prophylaxes. Pentamidine has no efficacy against toxoplasmosis and bacterial infections, which is of concern, especially after allogeneic HSCT [-]. Some authors have reported a mild to moderate decline in pulmonary function after long-term exposure [-], while others found no effect []. Pentamidine inhalation has been shown to cause considerable exposure and respiratory side effects in healthcare workers [, ], and adequate measures are recommended to protect staff. Our recommendation to use aerosolized pentamidine (300 mg once/month) is moderate (B-IIt)
claims.locator: Classen AY, Henze L, von Lilienfeld-Toal M, et al., AGIHO/DGHO, Annals of Hematology 100(6):1603 (doi 10.1007/s00277-021-04452-9), 'Primary prophylaxis of bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors: 2020 updated guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (AGIHO/DGHO)', published 2021 (2020 update), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116237/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Repeat imaging to follow response** (radiographic improvement at a median of 13 days). Do not use beta-D-glucan or BAL PCR to monitor treatment: both can stay positive after cure.
claims.source_text: Vogel et al. reported radiographic improvement becoming evident after a median of 13 days. … Monitoring therapy success using BDG or PCR-based DNA detection is not recommended as both can be elevated after successful treatment.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **HIV: start secondary prophylaxis straight after treatment and continue until CD4 is over 200 cells/mm³ for at least 3 months** (or CD4 100–200 with undetectable viral load for 3–6 months). Restart if CD4 falls below 100, or is 100–200 with detectable virus.
claims.source_text: In individuals with HIV, prophylaxis should be initiated immediately after completing PCP treatment and continued until the CD4 count exceeds 200 cells/mm³ for at least 3 months. In patients with a CD4 count between 100 and 200 cells/mm³ and undetectable viral RNA for 3-6 months, prophylaxis can also be discontinued. Regardless of viral load, secondary prophylaxis should be restarted if the CD4 count falls under 100 cells/mm³ or if it remains between 100 and 200 cells/mm³ with detectable viral RNA.
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Without HIV, secondary prophylaxis is also recommended after treatment,** stopping on an individual basis once immunity has recovered (ECIL). The transplant guideline (AST-IDCOP) does not recommend it for solid organ recipients.
claims.source_text: In non-HIV patients, secondary prophylaxis is also recommended after successful treatment of PCP. However, the recommendation on the duration remains vague. The ECIL guideline advises deciding on an individual basis once the immune system of the patients has fully recovered. … Although secondary prophylaxis is not recommended in SOT recipients
claims.locator: European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM), JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance 7(5):dlaf165, 'The 2025 EQUAL Pneumocystis Score—an ECMM tool to measure QUALity in Pneumocystis pneumonia management (Haensel L et al.)', published 29 September 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12477467/, retrieved 2026-09-23
